memo.verdict: Neutral; park, and more precisely close. The case is ended by a recommended, shareholder-approved scheme of arrangement and there is no action for Viewforth's capital at 6,430p (2026-09-22). DCC is a completed 'Major Corporate Change' that ended in a takeover rather than a re-rating; for a public holder today the shares are a five-month loan to the scheme paying about 3.6 to 8.4 percent a year, with about a one-in-ten chance of a 16 to 24 percent fall if the scheme fails. A holder from before April 2026 is being paid a fair price and should let the scheme complete; a buyer today earns an arbitrage spread with an adverse skew, which is not Viewforth's business. Conviction high on the verdict, because it rests on a contract and a vote, not a forecast. The park is on the return alone; the framework's gate (management, business quality, predictability, trackability) does not trigger it: management B, business quality B, predictability C, trackability B. Condition that would reopen the case: a scheme break, which would first take the shares to about 5,300p to 5,400p, from which the standalone case still returns only about 7 percent a year on the framework's valuation convention and clears the 20 percent bar only below about 4,530p, near the 52-week low of 4,187p. Neither entry level is available today. The primary 'Target Setup' is 'Major Corporate Change' at C for fit, with no secondary.
case: The change inside the company was as broad and as executed as the framework's screen asks for. In November 2024 DCC decided to sell Healthcare and Technology and become a pure-play energy distributor, then did it: Healthcare sold in September 2025 for £1,050m of enterprise value (about 12x 2024 operating profit, against a group multiple of about 9.5x; £945m net cash including £130m deferred); Info Tech sold to Aurelius in November 2025 for £100m of enterprise value; the Netherlands solar distribution business exited; Nexora, the remaining Technology business, for sale with an agreement targeted by the end of 2026; £700m returned in FY2026 (a £600m tender at £51.70 for 11.6m shares; a £100m buyback at an average £47.19), funded from disposal proceeds, with a final £100m scheduled for FY2028; finance and operating leadership changed in July 2025; four Central European markets entered in May 2026 ahead of schedule via UGI International's assets (more than 200m litres a year; 30,000 customers; AmeriGas Polska number two in Poland with 13 percent share); Progas in Germany bought for about £140m of enterprise value; the company renamed DCC Energy plc on 16 July 2026; full-time equivalents from 16,777 to 11,700. The screen's false-positive checks do not fire: no caretaker chief executive, no crown jewel sold cheaply, leverage 0.9x, buybacks not debt-funded. Three internal forces at A (strategy change, perimeter reduction, shareholder returns), five at B (other leaders, standards, new geographies, price rises, acquisitions), two at C (new products, balance sheet), two at D (no chief-executive change; guidance not raised), and the recommended acquisition itself at A as the thirteenth force, the strongest of all and terminal.

The outputs the change produced were modest, and the ones investors extrapolate barely moved. Continuing adjusted operating profit rose 3.6 percent to £634.0m in FY2026, organic +2.3 percent, about the historical average of 2.5 percent. Adjusted EPS rose 9.9 percent to 438.1p, mostly the tender's arithmetic (share count −13.7 percent; full-year accretion about 15.9 percent against operating profit growth of about 3 percent). Revenue fell 2.9 percent; core fuel volumes fell 3 percent; Mobility volumes fell 4.6 percent as management chose margin over volume. The replacement engine failed in the year it was meant to prove itself: Energy Services operating profit fell 67.5 percent to £15.7m, with a £43.16m Netherlands solar impairment and a £24.42m UK Services earn-out write-down; net operating exceptionals rose to £71.9m from £22.68m. Unit margins and cash were the bright outputs (Products operating profit per litre 3.3p to 3.8p; Mobility gross fuel margin 12.2p to 13.6p per litre; cash conversion 108 percent), but the research itself flags the cash as flattered by a £71.4m working-capital inflow from high oil prices, and the underlying conversion is nearer the chief financial officer's 90 percent standard. Consensus EPS drifted down over the year (FY2027 −1.5 percent; FY2028 −3.2 percent over twelve months); the sell-side never chased the story upward. Modal EPS growth is inside the 12 to 20 percent band only in FY2027 (+15.8 percent on consensus) and for the wrong reason; thereafter 5 to 6 percent a year on consensus (FY2028 +5.2 percent to £5.32; FY2029 +6.2 percent to £5.65) and 6 to 9 percent on the record's standalone path. The decomposition of the consensus three-year compound rate of 8.9 percent a year: revenue +2.3 percent a year (£15,442m to £16,515m); margin +1.3 percent a year (EBITDA £847m to £943m, +3.6 percent a year); below EBITDA +2.0 percent a year (lower depreciation after the Technology disposals; tax rising from 23.6 to about 25 percent); share count +3.1 percent a year; product 1.090, reconciling within rounding. The record's modal standalone path is about 7 to 8 percent a year FY2026 to FY2029, of which 3.1 points is the share count, so about 4 to 5 percent a year of operating growth.

The public market did not re-rate the equity for the simplification; private capital bid for it instead. The twelve-month-forward multiple had fallen from about 20x to about 10x over a decade and two years of break-up did not lift it. KKR and ECP approached at 5,800p in April 2026 and were refused; they agreed 6,525p in cash plus up to 125p contingent on the Nexora sale proceeds, a 24 percent premium to the undisturbed price, 7.5x CY2026 EV/EBITDA and 10.5x EV/EBIT, an equity value of about £5.75bn. Deutsche Bank calls the exit multiple virtually no premium to the conglomerate's historical average; the board told the offer negotiations that reaching the 2030 Ambition as a public company carried substantial execution risks. Recommendation 27 July 2026; ISS support 5 September 2026; the Court and General Meetings approved the scheme overwhelmingly on 18 September 2026; Fidelity (at £70), Ninety One, Aviva and Jim Flavin argued the price was too low and were outvoted; Davidson Kempner built 8.13 percent as an arbitrage position that wants completion.
counter_case: At its full force, the bull's case is that the public market has mispriced a structurally advantaged asset and the takeover proves it. DCC owns the tanks on about 1.5 million customers' sites with 10-to-20-year lives; it holds about 30 percent share in consolidated European liquid gas markets from which the oil majors have exited; it earns 18.8 percent pre-tax return on capital in Energy and has converted 98 percent of profit to cash for 32 years; its network is a low-cost base for the transition products (solar, heat pumps, HVO) that fragmented installers cannot match; the 2030 Ambition doubles operating profit to £830m and Jefferies thinks the M&A leg is conservative and could be reached two to three years early; a consortium with better information is paying 7.5x EBITDA and, on Deutsche Bank's arithmetic, expects a 20 percent IRR at 4x opening leverage; Fidelity said £70 was the floor and Ninety One, Aviva and the founder agreed; Davidson Kempner built 8.13 percent; and the exit multiple of 10.5x EV/EBIT is, by the bidders' own broker, no premium to the conglomerate average. On that view the equity is worth more than 6,525p, the scheme transfers value from public to private holders, and a shareholder who could block or outlast it would earn the difference. The record concedes every fact: the buyers probably earn their 20 percent; the public market never paid for the simplification; the board sold at the asset's historical multiple; on a break the assets would attract interest again.

The bull's bounded-downside claim, that Energy alone covers the enterprise value, is shown and fails. Energy adjusted operating profit was £554.2m in FY2026, an operating-profit line; the only enterprise-value-to-operating-profit multiple in the evidence is the offer's own 10.5x CY2026 EV/EBIT; at 10.5x Energy is worth £5,819m against an enterprise value of £6,367m at £64.25, a cover of 91 percent; the comparison set gives no enterprise multiple, the lowest in the research (UGI International at 6.0x EV/EBITDA) is on a different profit line with no Energy figure, so no like-for-like lower bound can be shown, and at any multiple below 10.5x the cover falls below 91 percent; the Technology business (about £800m on Jefferies; about £680m on Deutsche Bank at 8x) closes the gap and its sale is the contingent leg.
triggers: - Completion of the scheme (the Case/SP Key Driver; its inverse, a scheme break, the Case/SP Key Risk). Alarm: the spread to 6,525p wider than 3 percent without news; a delay announcement; a regulatory referral; a leveraged-buyout financing shock or a failed or repriced private-equity deal in European mid-caps. Invalidate: the scheme lapses or is withdrawn. The record's odds: completion about nine in ten; a break about one in ten, taking the shares to about 5,412p to 4,874p on today's earnings.

- The Nexora sale proceeds (Key Driver; inverse, a delay or shortfall, Key Risk). Alarm: no agreement announced by 31 December 2026. Invalidate: the sale abandoned, contingent nil. Expected about 50p of the up-to-125p; the full 125p about 30 percent; the sale announcement and its price would change the record's view of the payoff.

- The false friend on the standalone branch (Key Risk; matters only on a break). Alarm: a half-year core volume decline above 4 percent without margin offset. Invalidate: a quarterly core volume decline above 5 percent without margin offset. Watch core volumes against the 2 percent a year decline base, the working-capital reversal, exceptionals, Services organic growth and profit at the results of 10 November 2026.
- A warm winter before completion: a share-price risk only on a break; alarm a first-half FY2027 miss on 10 November 2026; heating degree days in the UK, France, Germany and the Nordics monthly.

- Where the shares settle on a break: about 5,300p to 5,400p; what would change the level is a second bidder or the company committing to lever up and buy back, which nothing in the evidence suggests.

- Not in the evidence and therefore unresolved: whether an interim dividend for the first half of FY2027 is permitted under the scheme (counted as nil); the remaining regulatory or financing conditions to completion (unnamed); the threshold of Nexora proceeds that pays the full 125p; the live thematics file, the track-record and lessons files and the Wisdom Library (the own-errors question not rated; the archetypes taken from the research); return on tangible capital (not disclosed).
